_link.title: I can describe the role of electric and magnetic fields in a synchrotron and explain why the magnetic field must increase as particles are accelerated

toLevel2.stem: What shape is the path that particles follow in a synchrotron?
distractors: A straight line forward
A spiral moving outward
A figure-eight pattern

toLevel2.stem: In a synchrotron, what type of field accelerates the particles to higher speeds?
distractors: Magnetic fields in curved sections
Gravitational fields at the centre
Thermal fields around the ring

toLevel2.stem: In a synchrotron, what type of field keeps the particles on a circular path?
distractors: Electric fields in straight sections
Gravitational fields at the centre
Frictional forces from the vacuum

toLevel2.stem: Why must the magnetic field in a synchrotron increase as particles are accelerated?
toLevel2.answer: To keep the orbital radius constant as speed increases
distractors: To prevent the particles from slowing down each lap
To increase the charge of the particles each orbit
To reduce the temperature inside the accelerator
Sydney
Canberra
Brisbane

toLevel2.stem: In a synchrotron, {{blank:1}} fields accelerate particles and {{blank:2}} fields bend them into a circular path.
As particle speed increases, the magnetic field must {{blank:1}} to maintain a {{blank:2}} orbital radius.
The Australian Synchrotron accelerates {{blank:1}} to nearly the speed of {{blank:2}}.
In a synchrotron, the magnetic field strength remains constant throughout the acceleration process.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: A synchrotron uses electric fields to increase the speed of charged particles.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Using r = mv/(qB), explain why B must increase when v increases to keep r constant.
toLevel3.answer: If v increases and r must stay constant, B must increase proportionally to compensate in the denominator
distractors: B must increase because the charge q decreases as the particle accelerates to higher speed
B must increase because the mass m decreases at higher speeds requiring a stronger field
B must increase because the radius r naturally increases and needs to be forced back down

toLevel3.stem: How does a synchrotron differ from a cyclotron?
toLevel3.answer: A synchrotron increases B to keep r constant, while a cyclotron has constant B and the radius increases with speed
distractors: A synchrotron uses only magnetic fields while a cyclotron uses only electric fields
A synchrotron has a fixed radius and fixed field; a cyclotron varies both continuously
A synchrotron accelerates protons only while a cyclotron accelerates electrons only

toLevel3.stem: What is synchrotron radiation and why does it occur?
toLevel3.answer: It is electromagnetic radiation emitted by charged particles undergoing centripetal acceleration in the magnetic field
distractors: It is heat generated by friction between the particles and the walls of the beam pipe
It is visible light produced when particles collide with gas molecules inside the ring
It is radiation from the magnets themselves as they increase their field strength

toLevel3.stem: Why is synchrotron radiation useful for scientific research?
toLevel3.answer: It produces intense, highly focused beams of radiation across a wide range of wavelengths from infrared to X-rays
distractors: It produces a single wavelength of visible light that is ideal for optical microscopy
It generates free electrons that can be used to power other laboratory instruments
It creates miniature magnetic fields that can be used to study atomic nuclei directly

toLevel3.stem: In a synchrotron, particles pass through RF (radio frequency) cavities. What do these cavities provide?
toLevel3.answer: An oscillating electric field that gives the particles a boost in energy each revolution
distractors: A steady magnetic field that keeps the particles on the correct circular path
A vacuum environment that prevents collisions between particles and air molecules
A cooling system that prevents the particles from overheating as they accelerate

toLevel3.stem: Why does a synchrotron have a fixed radius rather than allowing the radius to grow as in a cyclotron?
toLevel3.answer: A fixed radius allows a much smaller ring; only the magnets along the ring are needed rather than filling a large area
distractors: A fixed radius is required because the particles would escape if the radius changed
A fixed radius produces better synchrotron radiation because the curvature is constant
A fixed radius is used because it is impossible to make magnets that vary in strength

toLevel3.stem: From r = mv/(qB), keeping r constant while v increases requires B to {{blank:1}} in {{blank:2}} proportion to v.
Synchrotron radiation is emitted because the {{blank:1}} acceleration of the charged particles causes them to radiate {{blank:2}} energy.
RF cavities in a synchrotron provide an oscillating {{blank:1}} field that boosts the particle's {{blank:2}} each revolution.
A synchrotron keeps the orbital radius constant by increasing the magnetic field as particles speed up.
distractors: False

toLevel4.stem: An electron in a synchrotron is accelerated from 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s to 2.5 × 10⁸ m/s. By what factor must the magnetic field increase to maintain the same radius?
distractors: By a factor of 2.0
By a factor of 0.80
By a factor of 1.56

toLevel4.stem: The Australian Synchrotron has a ring diameter of approximately 70 m. If electrons travel at nearly 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, what is the approximate magnetic field strength needed? (m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, ignore relativistic effects)
distractors: Approximately 0.49 T
Approximately 4.9 T
Approximately 0.0049 T

toLevel4.stem: A synchrotron uses bending magnets and focusing magnets. What is the role of focusing magnets?
toLevel4.answer: To keep the beam tightly focused and prevent particles from drifting away from the ideal orbit
distractors: To accelerate the particles to higher speeds between the bending magnet sections
To reverse the direction of the beam so particles travel in the opposite direction
To slow down particles that are moving too fast for the ring to contain safely

toLevel4.stem: At the Australian Synchrotron, electrons are first accelerated in a linear accelerator (linac), then a booster ring, then the storage ring. Why is this multi-stage approach used?
toLevel4.answer: Each stage is optimised for a different energy range, making the overall acceleration more efficient and practical
distractors: A single stage cannot produce any magnetic field strong enough to bend electrons at all
Multiple stages are needed because electrons cannot be accelerated by electric fields alone
The multi-stage approach is used only for historical reasons and provides no actual benefit

toLevel4.stem: Synchrotron radiation causes energy loss. Calculate the energy that must be resupplied by the RF cavities if an electron loses 1.0 × 10⁻¹² J per revolution and completes 500,000 revolutions per second.
toLevel4.answer: 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ J per second (0.50 μW per electron)
distractors: 5.0 × 10⁵ J per second (500 kW per electron)
5.0 × 10⁻¹² J per second (5.0 pW per electron)
2.0 × 10⁻⁶ J per second (2.0 μW per electron)

toLevel4.stem: Why does synchrotron radiation pose a greater problem for electron synchrotrons than for proton synchrotrons?
toLevel4.answer: Radiation power scales as 1/m⁴, so the much lighter electron radiates enormously more power than a proton at the same energy
distractors: Electrons have a larger charge than protons so they experience more centripetal acceleration
Protons cannot emit synchrotron radiation because they are made of quarks not leptons
Electrons travel in smaller orbits than protons which makes them radiate less efficiently

toLevel4.stem: In the storage ring, the beam circulates for hours. Why must the vacuum be extremely good (ultra-high vacuum)?
toLevel4.answer: Even rare collisions with gas molecules would scatter electrons from the beam, gradually depleting it
distractors: The magnetic field cannot penetrate air so the ring must be evacuated for the magnets to work
The electric fields in the RF cavities would ionise any air present creating dangerous sparks
The synchrotron radiation would be absorbed by air molecules before reaching the beamlines

toLevel4.stem: If the speed of a particle doubles, the magnetic field must {{blank:1}} to keep the radius {{blank:2}}.
Synchrotron radiation is more problematic for {{blank:1}} than for protons because radiation power depends on the {{blank:2}} power of mass.
The multi-stage acceleration (linac → booster → storage ring) allows each stage to operate in its optimal {{blank:1}} range with appropriate {{blank:2}} strengths.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the trade-off between synchrotron radiation as an energy loss and as a useful research tool.
toLevel5.answer: While radiation represents an energy loss that must be compensated, it is precisely this radiation that makes the synchrotron valuable for research applications
distractors: Synchrotron radiation is purely a loss; all useful research applications use the electron beam directly
The radiation is always beneficial; the energy loss is negligible and requires no compensation
The trade-off does not exist because the radiation and the energy loss are completely unrelated

toLevel5.stem: Compare the advantages and limitations of a synchrotron versus a cyclotron for accelerating particles to very high energies.
toLevel5.answer: A synchrotron can reach much higher energies because it uses a fixed-size ring with increasing B, while a cyclotron's radius grows impractically large at high energies
distractors: A cyclotron is always superior because it does not need to change its magnetic field strength
Both are equally capable at all energies; the choice depends only on cost and availability
A synchrotron can only reach low energies while a cyclotron can accelerate to any energy

toLevel5.stem: At the Australian Synchrotron, electrons travel at 99.99999% of the speed of light. Analyse why the classical formula r = mv/(qB) is insufficient at this speed.
toLevel5.answer: At near-light speeds, relativistic mass increase means the momentum is much larger than mv predicts, requiring a much stronger B field
distractors: The formula is perfectly accurate at all speeds including those very close to the speed of light
At near-light speeds the charge of the electron decreases, making the formula give wrong results
The formula fails because magnetic fields cannot act on particles travelling this fast at all

toLevel5.stem: A physicist proposes building a synchrotron with a radius of 1.0 km to reduce synchrotron radiation losses. Evaluate this proposal.
toLevel5.answer: A larger radius reduces centripetal acceleration, decreasing radiation losses, but at enormous cost in construction and the number of magnets needed
distractors: A larger radius would increase radiation losses because particles travel a greater distance per lap
A larger radius has no effect on radiation because losses depend only on the particle's energy
A larger radius would eliminate radiation entirely because the path becomes essentially straight

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why the timing of the RF cavity oscillation must be precisely synchronised with the particle's orbital frequency.
toLevel5.answer: If the electric field is not correctly timed, it would decelerate the particles during some crossings, reducing their energy instead of increasing it
distractors: Timing does not matter because the electric field always accelerates regardless of direction
The timing must be precise only to prevent the particles from colliding with the cavity walls
The RF frequency determines the wavelength of synchrotron radiation, not the acceleration

toLevel5.stem: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) uses superconducting magnets with fields of about 8.3 T. Explain why such strong fields are necessary.
toLevel5.answer: The extremely high momentum of near-light-speed protons requires very strong B to maintain a fixed 27 km circumference orbit
distractors: Superconducting magnets are used only to save electricity, not because the field must be strong
Strong fields are needed to ionise the protons before they enter the accelerating sections
The 8.3 T field is needed to produce enough synchrotron radiation for the LHC experiments

toLevel5.stem: Compare how the Australian Synchrotron and the Large Hadron Collider use their accelerated particles differently.
toLevel5.answer: The Australian Synchrotron uses the synchrotron radiation emitted by electrons; the LHC collides protons to study fundamental particles
distractors: Both facilities use their particles in exactly the same way for identical types of research
The LHC uses synchrotron radiation while the Australian Synchrotron collides particles
Neither facility uses the accelerated particles directly; both study the magnetic fields only

toLevel5.stem: Predict what would happen in a synchrotron if the magnetic field failed to increase as particles were accelerated.
toLevel5.answer: The radius would increase with each energy boost, causing particles to spiral outward and hit the beam pipe wall
distractors: The particles would continue in the same orbit because inertia keeps them on the same path
The particles would slow down to compensate for the unchanged magnetic field strength
The particles would spiral inward toward the centre of the ring and collide with each other

toLevel5.stem: At relativistic speeds, the effective momentum is much {{blank:1}} than mv, requiring a correspondingly {{blank:2}} magnetic field to maintain the orbit.
If the magnetic field fails to increase with speed, the orbital radius will {{blank:1}}, causing the beam to {{blank:2}} the beam pipe.
